# ADR-0015: Core points first, so halo removal is two integers

> **Status:** accepted | **Date:** 2026-07-31

**References:** [ADR-0016](../adr/ADR-0016.md), [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec), [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo), [RFC-0002:C-MATERIALISATION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-materialisation), [ADR-0018](../adr/ADR-0018.md)

## Context

[RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 1 governs *which* points and attributes survive a halo: a halo point may be read, must
never be relabelled as a core point, and the halo attribute must be absent from a pipeline's final output.
Nothing in it says how the surviving points are produced. A throwaway prototype measured what that silence
costs.

(Item 1 has been rewritten twice since this decision was taken. [ADR-0016](../adr/ADR-0016.md) replaced a flat prohibition on
emitting halo points with the never-relabel rule described above, so that a chain of operators could carry a
halo between them; later, membership was defined *geometrically* — a point is core where its position lies
within the partition's bounds — which demoted the boolean attribute from the definition of
membership to a cache of it. Nothing here depends on which wording is in force: all three are silent on
production, and the second change strengthens rather than disturbs this decision, because the ordering it
fixes is the one part of item 1 that geometry cannot recover.)

The measurement compared, for each attribute, the address of the memory backing it before and after the halo
was removed. A changed address is proof the bytes were rewritten. Over the same eight-attribute batch:

- Removing the halo by **selecting points** on the halo attribute: **0 of 8** attributes kept their address.
  Every retained attribute was written again, at a cost proportional to the points *kept*, on every partition
  of every neighbourhood operation.
- Removing it by **reducing the batch to a range** of points: **8 of 8** kept their address. The reduction
  adjusted two integers.

Both produce identical output. Nothing in the results distinguishes them, which is why the expensive one is
the one that gets written: selecting points by predicate is the obvious way to express "these and not
those", and it is correct.

The range-based route is only available if the core points are contiguous, so the question is what guarantees
that. Traced end to end, the cheap route held all the way through: a partition built by a COPC-like source,
handed to a neighbourhood operator that read the halo, reduced to its core points, and delegated to an
analytical engine's aggregate, which returned the right count. The coordinate attribute's address in the batch
handed to the engine equalled its address in the source batch. No address was read from inside the engine's
own operator, so what is established is that nothing was copied *up to* the boundary — which is the part this
decision governs.

The operator in that trace is also where the general form of the problem showed itself. An operator that
rebuilds every output attribute value-by-value pays the same invisible cost for the same invisible reason,
whether or not a halo is involved. Rewritten to slice the attributes it passes through and materialise only
the neighbour count it derives, it wrote exactly one attribute — the derived one — while its four
pass-through attributes kept their addresses, and its results matched a whole-dataset reference exactly. The
earlier version rebuilt every attribute it emitted; its addresses were never captured, so the comparison is
one measured run against one inspected implementation rather than two measurements.

One limit belongs with the evidence rather than after it, and a later measurement changed its shape. The
figures above were obtained by comparing each attribute's *first* data buffer, over eight fixed-width
attributes. That check is insufficient in general: a follow-up exercised a nullable attribute and a struct
attribute and found the struct one reported *unchanged* by the first-buffer comparison while having been fully
rewritten — a struct array has no data buffers of its own, so the comparison inspects nothing and always
agrees. A transitive comparison over value buffers, validity bitmap and child arrays separated the two cases
correctly, which is why [RFC-0002:C-MATERIALISATION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-materialisation) 4 specifies it that way. Dictionary-encoded attributes
remain unexercised.

## Decision

Core points precede halo points within a batch, so removing a halo is a reduction to a range rather than a
selection over the whole batch. The obligations are written in [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) — item 1's ordering
bullet, and items 5 and 6 — and in [RFC-0002:C-MATERIALISATION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-materialisation); this ADR records only *why*. Item 1's
other bullets are [ADR-0016](../adr/ADR-0016.md)'s.

Why an **in-batch ordering contract** rather than the alternatives:

- **It is free where a partition is assembled.** A partition's own points are known before any neighbour is
  borrowed, so appending borrowed points after them is the natural construction order. The contract asks the
  assembling stage to keep an order it already has.
- **It keeps the operator's read view contiguous.** An operator reading a neighbourhood wants one view of
  core-plus-halo. Ordering delivers both that and a cheap removal from the same batch.
- **The halo attribute survives unchanged.** Membership itself is geometric rather than a property of the
  column, but the column that caches it stays an ordinary one, so an external Arrow consumer reads it without
  knowing anything about Strider ([RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 3) while Strider reads the same fact as a point count.

- **A halo stays ordinary data, and that is what keeps the operator contract uniform.** One batch means an operator receives points, some of which are halo, and nothing about its input shape depends on whether it asked for a halo. An operator declaring zero halo width is handed no halo points and needs no notion of them; one declaring a width is handed them in the same batch it was already reading. Two batches invert this: every operator's read path has to contemplate a second input, including the operators that never wanted one, so the arrangement that is cheaper at removal is the one that pushes a case distinction into code that has no interest in the distinction. Since halo membership became geometric ([ADR-0018](../adr/ADR-0018.md)), this is the argument the decision principally rests on — a uniform contract rather than a judgement about who writes operators.

Why the ordering is **verified rather than assumed** ([RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 5): a plain Arrow batch cannot
express row order in its schema, which is the price of [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 3's no-envelope rule. So the contract is
invisible to every producer that might break it — a source reading in storage order, a repartitioning, an
engine's sort — and a mis-ordered batch reduced to a range emits halo points and drops core points while
returning a plausible count. The check is cheap, and it is the only thing between the cheap implementation
and a silent wrong answer.

Why the general rule is a **separate clause**: the prohibition on rewriting a passed-through attribute has no
halo content and applies to every operator. Keeping it in [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) would have made an assessor
open a clause about neighbourhoods to find an obligation about operators generally, and would have left the
project's throughput claim with no home of its own.

## Consequences

### Positive

Halo removal stops *writing* anything: its cost falls from rewriting every retained attribute to adjusting an
offset and a length, plus one read pass over the halo attribute to verify the ordering. Combined with
[RFC-0002:C-MATERIALISATION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-materialisation) 1, a neighbourhood operator's cost is the arithmetic it actually does plus the
attributes it actually derives, and nothing on the measured path to a delegated aggregate is copied.
The obligation is checkable by a test that can fail, which a value comparison could not be. Nothing about the
interoperability surface changes: the halo attribute is still an ordinary column.

### Negative

An unstated ordering contract becomes a stated one, and it binds a wider set of code than the clause that
needs it — any stage assembling a partition has to preserve it, and the batch itself cannot carry the
requirement because [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 3 forbids an envelope. Every halo removal now pays a verification
pass over the halo attribute, which is cheap but not free, and which the previous select-based implementation
did not need because it could not be wrong in this way.

Where core and halo points genuinely arrive interleaved — read in storage order, or inherited from a
repartitioning — establishing the order costs exactly the rewrite this decision exists to avoid. The
obligation is scoped to the batch handed to an operator for that reason, which means a source cannot always
hand its output straight to an operator without an assembling stage in between.

[RFC-0002:C-MATERIALISATION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-materialisation) 3 also has to carve out spill and serialisation, since memory identity cannot
survive either, and that carve-out is a place a future implementation could hide: spilling to escape a
sharing obligation is forbidden, but only by a sentence.

The safety case rests on a verification whose obvious implementation reports success falsely. Comparing one
buffer per attribute is the natural way to check memory identity, and it passes vacuously for a struct
attribute and inspects only offsets for a variable-length or dictionary-encoded one — measured, not
supposed. Those are the attribute shapes a real point cloud acquires as it gains richer per-point data, so
the failure mode gets more likely rather than less. [RFC-0002:C-MATERIALISATION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-materialisation) 4 requires the transitive
comparison for this reason, and an implementation that reads the obligation quickly will get it wrong in the
direction that reports conformance.

Separate core and halo batches would make removal free and need no ordering contract at all, so the option not
taken is the cheaper one at the point of removal. This paragraph originally recorded that its rejection rested
on a judgement about operator authors rather than on a measurement, and set a revisit trigger: whether an
operator can tolerate a two-batch input. That trigger has fired, and what it produced needs stating carefully,
because the first attempt to state it was wrong.

Operators tolerate it, and one recorded objection was simply false. It said a two-batch operator must either
handle two batches throughout or concatenate them. A third arrangement was not considered: global indices over a
conceptual join, resolved by a branch at the coordinate fetch. Measured, that produced results identical to the
single-batch form over a real partition and a spatial index of identical size, with nothing concatenated and
nothing copied.

**The cost this paragraph briefly claimed does not survive measurement.** A first attempt reported the branch
costing about a sixth of the neighbourhood computation. That figure came from splitting a uniformly random cloud
three-quarters of the way through and calling the tail a halo, which scatters halo points across the whole
extent and leaves almost every grid cell holding a random mixture — so the branch mispredicted on nearly every
candidate. A real halo is a boundary shell: interior cells are wholly core, only cells near the partition
boundary are mixed, and the branch becomes predictable. Measured over a genuine partition in a release build,
the two arrangements are indistinguishable — between 0.98 and 1.00 times the single-batch time over four runs,
with the two-batch form marginally ahead. The earlier figure also survived into debug builds and that apparent
agreement across profiles was cited as proof the cost was arithmetic rather than an artefact; on real geometry
the profiles disagree, release showing no cost and debug still showing about 1.15.

So the position is this. The objection about concatenation is retired as false, and the measured cost is retired as an artefact. What the decision rests on instead is the uniformity argument in the decision above: a halo carried in the batch is ordinary data, so no operator's input shape depends on whether it asked for one, while two batches put a second input in front of every operator including those that declare no halo. That is a claim about the operator contract rather than a prediction about who writes operators, which is what the earlier framing got wrong in calling it a judgement about authors. It remains unmeasured — no operator exists yet to be made simpler or harder — so it is an argument from the shape of the interface, weighed against a removal cost that measurement has now shown to be nil either way.

### Neutral

Nothing here changes any result. Every obligation in this decision is about how many times bytes are
written, and a conformant implementation and a forbidden one agree on every value — which is the whole reason
the verification has to compare memory rather than output.

The decision does not bear on operators whose surviving points are not contiguous. Cropping to an arbitrary
region or filtering on an attribute must gather, and [RFC-0002:C-MATERIALISATION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-materialisation) 1 holds such an operator
only to gathering once.

Reversal cost is asymmetric, and the expensive direction is adoption rather than abandonment. Introducing the
ordering *after* sources, partitioners and repartitioners exist means auditing every one of them for an
invariant none was written to maintain, with no schema-level signal to audit against — which is the argument
for stating it now, while the only producer is a prototype. Abandoning it later is cheap by comparison:
reinstating a select-based removal is additive and local, and costs throughput rather than correctness.

## Alternatives Considered

### Order core points before halo points within a batch, and remove a halo by reducing the batch to that range (accepted)

- **Pros:** Measured: 7 of 7 attributes kept their backing memory across a removal that also drops the halo column, and 8 of 8 across the slice alone, against 0 of 8 for the select-based route, Free at the point of construction, since a partition's own points are known before any neighbour is borrowed, The operator still sees one contiguous view of core-plus-halo, so the read path costs nothing either, The halo attribute stays an ordinary column, so [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 3's no-envelope interoperability is untouched, Traced end to end: the coordinate attribute's address inside a delegated aggregate equalled its address at decode
- **Cons:** Introduces a semantic contract a plain Arrow batch cannot express in its schema, so it is invisible to producers that might break it, Binds every stage that assembles a partition, not only the stage that removes the halo, Requires a verification pass on every removal, because a mis-ordered batch reduced to a range fails silently, Costs a full rewrite where core and halo points genuinely arrive interleaved

### Remove the halo by selecting points on the halo attribute, and accept the rewrite (rejected)

- **Pros:** No ordering contract, so nothing invisible to break and nothing to verify, Works whatever order the points arrive in, including interleaved, The obvious implementation, and correct — it is what the prototype's own guard rule did
- **Cons:** Measured: 0 of 8 retained attributes kept their backing memory; every one was written again, The cost is proportional to the points KEPT, and is paid on every partition of every neighbourhood operation, Invisible: output is identical, so no result-level test can ever reveal it
- **Rejected because:** The discriminator is that its cost is invisible: output is identical, so no result-level test can ever reveal it, and a project claiming out-of-core processing can be fast rather than merely possible would be shipping a default path that copies the data on every partition of every neighbourhood operation with nothing to signal it. That it rewrites every retained attribute to drop a quarter of a batch's points is the measurement; that nothing would ever tell you is the reason.

### Supply core points and halo points as separate batches, so removing the halo is dropping a batch (rejected)

- **Pros:** Cheapest of all: removal is discarding a reference, with not even a range to compute, Needs no in-batch ordering contract, so nothing invisible to break and no verification pass, Satisfies [RFC-0002:C-MATERIALISATION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-materialisation) 2 trivially, since no batch is reduced at all, Measured: needs no concatenation — a virtual index space over two arrays gives identical results and a byte-identical spatial index, Measured over a real partition in release: indistinguishable from the single-batch form, 0.98 to 1.00x, so the fetch branch costs nothing where halo points form a boundary shell
- **Cons:** Splits one contract into two shapes: 'a batch' stops being what an operator consumes, so every rule quantifying over batches must say which of the pair it means, Every operator's read path must contemplate a second input, including operators that declare no halo and have no interest in the distinction
- **Rejected because:** Two of its three original objections have fallen. The one about sitting awkwardly with a per-point halo attribute lapsed once membership was defined geometrically and the attribute became a cache of it, which [ADR-0018](../adr/ADR-0018.md) argues — still proposed, so that first ground remains provisional, though the third below does not depend on it. The one about needing concatenation was wrong: global indices over a conceptual join need neither a join nor a copy, and were measured giving identical results over a real partition with an equally sized index and no measurable difference in time.

What survives is the third, though not on the ground first given. The objection is not that a two-batch input falls on whoever writes a neighbourhood operator — that is a prediction about authors, and this decision no longer rests on it. It is that a second input changes the operator **contract**, uniformly and for everyone: one batch in and one batch out stops being the shape an operator consumes, so every operator's read path must contemplate a pair, including operators that declare no halo and have no interest in the distinction, and every rule elsewhere in the corpus that quantifies over a batch has to say which of the pair it means. Ordering within a single batch confines the cost to the stages that assemble a partition and the stage that removes a halo, and leaves the contract one shape.
